analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell prescriptions to pharmacies at foreign prices for Medicare patients.
analysis.headline: The bill, which aimed to cut Medicare patients' drug prices by an estimated 40%, never received a committee hearing, floor vote, or a single cosponsor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced drug manufacturers that sell to the federal government to also sell their drugs to pharmacies, for Medicare patients, at no more than the average price the company charges in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The bill's findings said older Americans often pay twice as much, and sometimes ten times as much, as those customers. Companies that refused to comply would be barred from federal contracts. The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans at the time, who pay for prescriptions out of pocket; the bill estimated their drug prices would fall by about 40% on average. Taxpayers would also benefit if Medicare paid less for drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Pharmacies could buy drugs for Medicare beneficiaries at no more than the manufacturer's average foreign price, calculated across Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the United Kingdom, including rebates and discounts. [S3]

The bill's findings estimated implementation would cut prescription drug prices for many Medicare beneficiaries by an average of 40 percent, citing instances where older Americans pay up to ten times what the industry's most favored customers pay. [S3]
Manufacturers that did not comply would be debarred from federal contracting, enforced through the government's purchasing power, and the bill included hospice patients among those covered. [S3]
The Secretary would have to report to Congress annually on whether the law was reducing prices, with recommendations for further cuts. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose United States sales prices for Medicare patients would be pulled down toward lower foreign price levels, reducing revenue on those sales.

drawbacks.text: The bill used only the government's contracting power: it applied to manufacturers that sell covered drugs to the United States, so its reach over a company's prices depended on the Secretary's implementation choices. [S3]

Drug makers would argue that foreign price controls let other governments charge less while American sales fund research into new medicines, so pegging US prices to foreign averages could reduce industry revenue and slow new drug development; the bill text does not address that trade-off. [S3]

Lower prices depend on the average foreign price definition working in practice across six countries with different pricing systems, which the Secretary would have to untangle through regulations. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare patients the potential gain was large — roughly a 40% price cut on out-of-pocket drugs by the bill's own estimate — and it would be paid almost entirely by drug manufacturers' margins, not by taxpayers. The main honest cost is the industry's argument that foreign prices are kept low by other governments and that US prices partly fund new drug development; the bill offered no offsetting mechanism for that concern, so it was a blunt instrument. Still, the distribution of the trade-off favored ordinary patients over a concentrated industry.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced it, the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Johnson introduced the bill on April 11, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee. [S5]
No other senator cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill's complete action history ends with the referral. [S5]
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill did not carry over. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: American Medicare patients continued paying substantially more for the same drugs than customers in Canada, Japan, and Europe, without any price floor ever coming to a vote.

for.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over Medicare and drug pricing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 11, 2003 and never held a markup, hearing action, or sent it to the floor.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Would have faced mandatory foreign-price caps on sales to Medicare patients and debarring from federal contracts; the industry opposed foreign price references in this era, though no lobbying record appears in this bill's file.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split ever formed on the record; it never advanced far enough for a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped their effective US sales prices to Medicare patients at the average foreign price across six countries, with federal debarment as the penalty for noncompliance. Their US revenue, historically higher than foreign prices, would have been reduced. [S3]
Pharmacies would have gained access to Medicare-patient volumes of drugs at lower wholesale prices, potentially widening margins on senior customers or passing the savings on. [S3]
